findings.claim: For Edexcel 1ET0 Component 2, Section A ... Part (a) ... (AO1 + AO2). Part (b) asks you to explore a theme, character, or idea across the whole novella (AO1 + AO2).
findings.truth: On the Edexcel 19th-century novel question part (a) is 20 marks for AO2 alone and part (b) is 20 marks for AO1 alone. The old text gave both parts AO1 + AO2. 'Edexcel 1ET0' and 'Component 2' are also banned strings that fail the house validator.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md L1161-1172 ('students complete a two part question ... Assessment Objectives covered are AO1 and AO2') and the raw-mark table L1340-1360 (Questions 1a-7a: AO2 20; 1b-7b: AO1 20).

findings.claim: Practice question 5: 'Read the following extract from Chapter 10: The moment I choose, I can be rid of Mr Hyde.'
findings.truth: Jekyll says this to Utterson in Chapter 3 ('Dr Jekyll Was Quite at Ease'), not in the Chapter 10 confession. The point of the line is its early confidence, so the chapter matters.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #43 line 649, inside the chapter that starts at line 590 'DR. JEKYLL WAS QUITE AT EASE'.

findings.claim: Practice question 3: 'Read the following extract from Chapter 10: The moment I choose, I can be rid of Mr Hyde.'
findings.truth: Same misattribution as F1 above: the line is Chapter 3.

findings.claim: Jekyll's statement ends mid-sentence. He writes: 'I bring the life of that unhappy Henry Jekyll to an end.' (repeated in flashcard 11: 'Mid-sentence - ...')
findings.truth: The confession ends with a complete, composed sentence: 'Here then, as I lay down the pen and proceed to seal up my confession, I bring the life of that unhappy Henry Jekyll to an end.' Nothing breaks off. The claim also contradicts the quotation printed beside it.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #43 lines 2578-2579, the last lines of the novella.

findings.claim: Eight months later, Hyde commits a far more terrible crime.
findings.truth: Chapter 4 opens 'Nearly a year later, in the month of October'. The gap is close to a year, not eight months.

findings.claim: half the rooms are furnished with luxury and good taste, while the other half are in disarray (repeated in flashcard 12: 'Half luxurious ...; half chaotic')
findings.truth: Hyde used only a couple of rooms and both were furnished with luxury and good taste; the disorder is a hurried ransacking of those same rooms, not a second half of the flat. The lesson invents a spatial split that is not in the text.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #43 lines 806-816: 'Mr. Hyde had only used a couple of rooms; but these were furnished with luxury and good taste ... At this moment, however, the rooms bore every mark of having been recently and hurriedly ransacked'.

findings.claim: The maidservant is one of only two women in the entire novella (the other is the girl Hyde tramples).
findings.truth: At least three women appear. The old woman who keeps Hyde's Soho lodgings has a speaking scene with Utterson and the inspector, and Chapter 1 also has the women of the trampled girl's family.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #43 lines 799-806 ('A flash of odious joy appeared upon the woman's face ... which but for the old woman remained otherwise empty').

findings.claim: She watches the murder from a window 'romantically given' and by the light of a full moon.
findings.truth: 'Romantically given' describes the maid, not the window: 'It seems she was romantically given, for she sat down upon her box'. As printed, the lesson hangs the quotation on the wrong noun.

findings.claim: He finds Jekyll in his cabinet ... looking 'deadly sick.'
findings.truth: The text reads 'there, close up to the warmth, sat Dr. Jekyll, looking deathly sick'. 'Deadly sick' is a misquotation of a memorisable phrase in a closed-book paper.

findings.claim: he is compared to a 'troglodyte' (also in the lesson 1 conclusion and in lesson 7 content)
findings.truth: The word 'troglodyte' never appears. Utterson thinks 'Something troglodytic, shall we say?' in Chapter 2. Three occurrences corrected to 'troglodytic'.

findings.claim: Jekyll's house is in a wealthy, respectable area (loosely based on Cavendish Square). Flashcard 5 asks which square holds Jekyll's front entrance and answers 'a wealthy square modelled loosely on Cavendish Square'.
findings.truth: Cavendish Square is Lanyon's address in the novella - 'Cavendish Square, that citadel of medicine, where his friend, the great Dr. Lanyon, had his house'. Jekyll's square is never named; it is 'a square of ancient, handsome houses, now for the most part decayed from their high estate'.

findings.claim: When the fog lifts briefly during the Carew murder, the moonlight reveals the violence that normally remains hidden.
findings.truth: The fog had not yet arrived. 'Although a fog rolled over the city in the small hours, the early part of the night was cloudless, and the lane ... was brilliantly lit by the full moon.' The murder happens before the fog, so nothing lifts.

findings.claim: Printed extract: 'A closet filled with wine; the plate was of silver ...'
findings.truth: The text reads 'A closet was filled with wine'. A printed extract set for close language analysis must be verbatim.

findings.claim: Printed extract: '... of the two natures that contended in the field of my consciousness, if I could rightly be said to be either ...'
findings.truth: The text reads 'even if I could rightly be said to be either'. The dropped word changes the concessive sense of the clause.

findings.claim: All 42 practice questions carry the label '20 marks - Extract Analysis', including the 21 that ask for a whole-novella essay (e.g. 'Explore how Stevenson presents the theme of duality in the novella as a whole').
findings.truth: Those 21 are part (b) whole-text essays, not extract analysis. Relabelled '20 marks - Whole-Text Essay', matching the fix already applied to the sister Edexcel novel units (a-christmas-carol, jane-eyre). Three per lesson, indices 1, 3 and 5.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md L1161-1170 ('Part 1 is focussed on a close language analysis of an extract ... Part 2 questions may focus on ... plot, setting(s), character(s), theme(s)').

findings.claim: Every mark scheme uses the ladder Top band / Upper-mid band / Lower-mid band / Lower band.
findings.truth: 'Lower band' is not on the house ladder (Top / Upper-mid / Mid / Lower-mid / Low / Basic), and the 'Mid band' rung is missing entirely. 42 mark schemes are affected. Left to the fleet-wide band-ladder relabel rather than edited here.

findings.claim: He describes the 'leap of welcome' he felt with each transformation (also lessons 5 and 7).
findings.truth: The phrase is used once, for Jekyll's first sight of Hyde in the mirror: 'when I looked upon that ugly idol in the glass, I was conscious of no repugnance, rather of a leap of welcome'. Not 'each transformation'. The wider point (Jekyll enjoyed being Hyde) is supported elsewhere, so no edit.

findings.claim: Flashcard: 'What physical adjective does Stevenson repeatedly use to describe Hyde?' -> 'Dwarfish.'
findings.truth: 'Dwarfish' appears once ('Mr. Hyde was pale and dwarfish'); Poole's 'more of a dwarf' is the only echo. 'Repeatedly' overstates it, but the answer itself is right, so no edit.

findings.claim: Flashcard: 'Which Jekyll confession opens Chapter 10 with the novella's central statement?'
findings.truth: 'Man is not truly one, but truly two' comes about a page into Chapter 10, which opens 'I was born in the year 18- to a large fortune'. The answer is right; only the stem's 'opens' is loose.

findings.claim: Glossary: cyanide = 'A chemical compound containing cyanide, used as a fast-acting poison.'
findings.truth: Circular definition. The reading itself is sound - the text gives 'the strong smell of kernels' beside the crushed phial - so this is a wording defect, not a factual error.

summary: Seven lessons checked against the Edexcel 1ET0 spec and Gutenberg #43. Four HIGH findings: the exam paragraph gave both parts AO1 + AO2 (part (a) is AO2 only, part (b) AO1 only) and carried two banned spec/component codes; 'The moment I choose, I can be rid of Mr Hyde' is set as a Chapter 10 extract twice when it is Chapter 3; and Jekyll's confession is said to end mid-sentence when it ends with a complete sentence. Ten more real errors follow the sister-unit pattern - 21 whole-text essays labelled 'Extract Analysis', the Carew murder dated eight months rather than nearly a year on, an invented half-luxury/half-chaos split in Hyde's Soho rooms, 'only two women in the novella', 'deadly sick' for 'deathly sick', 'troglodyte' for 'troglodytic', and Cavendish Square given to Jekyll when it is Lanyon's. No lesson is clean; every lesson carries at least the mislabelled practice questions.
